statement: Nina knows the answer to a contest question is even and bigger than 7. The choices are 2, 8, 9, 10 and 13. How many choices can she be sure are wrong?

choices.misconception: I only crossed out a choice if it broke both facts, and no choice breaks both.
I crossed out only 2, the choice that is 7 or less, and forgot to cross out the odd numbers.
I crossed out only the odd numbers, 9 and 13, and forgot that 2 is not bigger than 7.
I also crossed out 8, because I mixed up bigger than 7 with bigger than 8.

hints: Cross out every choice that breaks one of the two facts.
Each fact lets you cross out choices: one removes the odd numbers, the other removes the numbers that are 7 or less. A choice that breaks either fact must be wrong.
The odd choices are 9 and 13. Which other choice is 7 or less?

solutions.reliable: 9 and 13 are odd, so they are wrong. 2 is even but not bigger than 7, so it is wrong too. That makes 3 choices Nina can cross out: 2, 9 and 13. Only 8 and 10 are left, and she should guess one of them, because a blank can never score. The idea to keep: crossing out impossible choices turns a wild guess into a much better one.

whyOnTest: Contest craft: a wrong answer costs nothing, so crossing out impossible choices and then guessing always beats leaving a blank.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
